messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Parole Officer
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 67

He is 34, an African man who works as a parole officer, and when he first begins talking about what happened, he does so in the same controlled tone he uses at work when he needs to calm an agitated client. He is careful with his words. He tends to describe events as if they happened to someone else. Only gradually does the story become personal.

He meets his partner three years ago. In the beginning, he experiences the relationship as intense, affectionate, and fast-moving. She calls often, wants to know where he is, tells him she has never felt so understood. He interprets her jealousy as closeness. He works long days supervising people recently released from custody, and he is used to conflict, deception, and volatility in his job. At home, he tells himself, things are simply passionate. When she becomes angry if he comes back late from field visits or if he does not answer during meetings, he apologizes quickly and tries to keep the peace.

The first time she hits him, they are in her apartment kitchen. He has mentioned that he may need to work overtime because one of his clients has violated parole conditions. She accuses him of lying and seeing someone else. Before he fully understands the shift in her face, she throws a mug that strikes his shoulder, then slaps him hard across the mouth. He stands there stunned, tasting blood, more confused than angry. What comes to him first is embarrassment. He is a large man, physically strong, someone who spends his workdays assessing risk and setting limits. He cannot make sense of being afraid in his own relationship. The next morning she cries, says she was under stress, says he knows how to push her buttons. He accepts the apology and does not tell anyone.

After that, he begins organizing his life around her moods. He checks his phone constantly during work. If he sees several missed calls from her while he is in court or in a case conference, his stomach drops. He steps into hallways to call her back, lowering his voice, assuring her where he is. Coworkers notice he has become distracted. He starts making small mistakes in documentation, unusual for him. He tells himself he is just tired.

The violence becomes more frequent over the next year. She shoves him, scratches his neck, once corners him near the front door and punches him in the ribs while accusing him of disrespecting her. He never strikes back. He says his body goes rigid, as though any movement might make things worse. Sometimes he leaves and sits in his car for an hour, gripping the steering wheel until the shaking stops. Sometimes he stays, trying to talk her down, using the same measured language he uses with clients in crisis. Later he feels humiliated by this instinct, as if he has become an officer in his own home, forever assessing danger, scanning tone, watching hands.

He becomes increasingly isolated. He stops seeing friends because she questions him afterward for hours. He avoids calling his family because he does not want them to hear the strain in his voice. In his community, and in his own thinking, there is a deep shame attached to being a man who is hurt by a partner. He worries no one will believe him, or worse, that they will laugh. At work he presents as composed and capable. At home he feels himself shrinking.

One night, after an argument about a female colleague whose name appears in a work email, she strikes him repeatedly with the metal end of a phone charger and then locks the door when he tries to leave. He remembers the sound of his own breathing more than anything else—fast, shallow, animal-like. He is suddenly certain that if he does not get out, something irreversible will happen. When she turns away for a second, he pulls the door open and runs down the stairs. Outside, he vomits in the bushes. For a long time afterward, he cannot tolerate the buzz of a phone charger cable brushing against a wall without feeling his chest seize.

Since leaving the relationship, he says he is no longer living with daily violence, but his body does not seem to know that. He sleeps lightly and wakes at small sounds, already braced. If his current partner raises her voice in ordinary frustration, he feels a flash of heat and panic and has to fight the urge to leave the room immediately. He avoids streets near his former partner’s apartment and checks parking lots before getting out of his car. At home he sits facing the door in restaurants and notices exits automatically, something he used to do only during fieldwork.

Nights are the hardest. He has recurring dreams in which he is back in the apartment, unable to open the door, his hands clumsy and weak. He wakes sweating, heart pounding, and then stays awake listening for sounds that do not come. In the morning he feels ashamed of how exhausted he is. He has become more irritable, especially at work, where angry clients can suddenly remind him of her expression just before she attacked him. On those days he feels himself split in two: outwardly professional, inwardly back in that kitchen, or by that locked door, waiting for the next blow.

What troubles him most is not only fear but the damage to his sense of himself. He used to think of himself as steady under pressure, someone other people relied on for safety and structure. Now he questions his judgment constantly. He replays the relationship, searching for the moment he should have recognized the danger, the moment he should have left. He says he knows, logically, that he survived repeated abuse. But emotionally he still lives as though violence is just about to happen again.
